_comment: ElevenLabs Sound Effects settings. Like the voice block, everything here is part
of the SFX cache fingerprint, so changing a value regenerates the assets it
affects and nothing else. No secret belongs in this file.
`model` is deliberately null: an unset model means the provider's own default,
which is better than inventing a model id. The fingerprint records null as a
value, so naming a model later invalidates the assets and nothing before that.
promptMaxCharacters is 400, measured rather than documented. A 476-character
prompt was rejected twice with HTTP 400 -- at 22 seconds and again at 20 -- while
every asset at 385 characters or fewer generated first time, including a
20-second looping bed. So the boundary is somewhere between 386 and 475 and 400 is
a safe ceiling. Validation now catches an over-long prompt for free instead of
spending a call to discover it.
durationLimitsSeconds.max stays at 20 because 20 is proven for a looping bed; 22
has never been shown to work and is not worth a call to find out.
ONE EXCEPTION to the fingerprint line above, and it is deliberate: the `normalize`
block is NOT part of the fingerprint. Its own comment says why -- a level is baked
into the file after generation, so changing the target re-encodes what is already
on disk and never buys the asset again. sfx.fingerprint() names its inputs
explicitly, which is what keeps that true rather than hopeful.
Level baked into the asset FILE after generation, because neither prompting nor
the player can do it. ElevenLabs returns a one-off event at whatever level the
prompt implies but returns a continuous texture -- room tone, channel hiss, a
castor rumble, a stream of keystrokes -- near the noise floor whatever the prompt
says; two rounds of prompt work moved that group about 2 dB. And HTML `volume` is
capped at 1.0, so a cue gain can only ever attenuate.
So the asset is normalised and the cue gain goes back to being a MIX decision.
targetRmsDbfs is where a normalised asset lands: loud enough to sit under speech
at about -22 dBFS without disappearing. peakCeilingDbfs is the harder constraint --
the applied gain is the smaller of what the target asks and what the peak allows,
so a transient-heavy one-shot never clips. Raising is the default and attenuation
is opt-in, so nothing already approved gets quieter by accident.
maxGainDb is a refusal, not a clamp: a file needing more than 40 dB is broken
rather than quiet, and amplifying it 40 dB would deliver 40 dB of hiss.
peakCeilingDbfs IS -3, NOT -1, AND THE RESULT IS CHECKED AGAINST IT. mp3 is lossy:
a decode reconstructs more than the encoder was given. The first real pass aimed
eleven assets at -1.0 and delivered eleven files clamped at 0.0 dBFS, overshooting
by 1.0 to 2.8 dB. So -3 is the headroom the codec needs, and the pass no longer
trusts its own arithmetic: it measures the encoded file and backs the gain off
until the DELIVERED peak is under the ceiling, up to maxCorrections times.
Starting philosophy, not final artistic levels. Voice is the reference and is
never attenuated; everything else is set relative to it and is meant to be
retuned by ear without regenerating a single asset.
A cue's own `gain` wins over `categoryGain`. `duckUnderSpeechTo` is a MULTIPLIER
applied to a sustained bed while a voice clip is playing, so an alarm can be
loud in the gaps and still sit under the dialogue. One-shot foley is not ducked;
it is short enough to read through speech and ducking it would make it mush.
ambience ducks to 0.70 rather than 0.55 after Joshua's first listen: at 0.55 of an
already-quiet bed the room tone was inaudible under speech, which is the opposite
of what a bed is for. It still loses a third of its level while a voice sounds.
